chapters.title: Automation, blueprints and webhooks
intro: This chapter is for administrators. It explains rules, which automate routine work, and blueprints, which guide tickets through fixed steps. It also covers webhooks, which send events to other systems.
Every rule and blueprint has versions. You can test a change before it goes live, and you can go back to an earlier version.

sections.title: The Automation page
intro: To open automation, select **Automation** in the rail. You can also select **Administration** > **Automation & blueprints**.
You need the **Manage automation rules and blueprints** permission. The **Webhooks** tab appears only if you may also manage integrations.

blocks.alt: Automation page on the Rules tab with numbered highlights on the tabs, the search box, the trigger list, New rule, the first rule, its counts, its switch and its arrows

callouts: The tabs: **Rules**, **Executions**, **Blueprints** and **Webhooks**.
**Search rules** finds rules by name or description.

**New rule** opens the rule designer.
The rule's name, its description and its badges.

The switch turns the rule on or off. You can switch on a rule only after you publish it.
The arrows move the rule earlier or later within its trigger.

sections.title: How rules work
intro: A rule has three parts. **When** is the trigger, the event that starts the rule. **If** holds the conditions the ticket must meet. **Then** lists the actions that run, in order.
For example: when a ticket is created, and it is High priority from a VIP customer, raise it to Critical. Then notify a supervisor.
blocks: Rules with the same trigger run in the order shown on the **Rules** tab. A rule with **Stop processing later rules when this rule matches** ends the run for that event when it matches.
Each save creates a new version. Only the published version runs. You can test a draft first, then publish it.

list: Each event runs each rule version only once.
A rule never reacts to changes made by its own actions.
Chains of rules that start other rules stop after five steps.
One rule runs at most 20 times an hour on the same ticket.
A scheduled run handles at most 500 tickets.

blocks.note: Rules cannot delete tickets, merge them or mark them as spam. Agents do those things by hand.

sections.title: Create a rule
sections.intro: Create a rule to make SupportDesk act on tickets for you.
prerequisites: You have the **Manage automation rules and blueprints** permission.
steps: Select **Automation** > **Rules**, then select **New rule**.
Enter a **Rule name** and, if you like, a **Description**.
In the **When** card, select the trigger. See [Rule triggers](#au-triggers).
In the **If** card, add the conditions. See [Rule conditions](#au-conditions).
In the **Then** card, select **Add action** and choose an action. Fill in its fields.
Add more actions if you need them. Use the arrows to change their order.
If later rules must not run when this one matches, turn on **Stop processing later rules when this rule matches**.
Optionally enter a **Change note (optional)** that says what you changed.
Select **Save draft**.
sections.result: The app shows **Draft v1 saved**. The draft does not run yet. Test it, then publish it. See [Simulate a rule](#au-simulate-rule) and [Check and publish a rule](#au-publish-rule).

sections.title: Rule triggers
sections.intro: The trigger is the event that starts a rule. You choose one trigger per rule in the **When** card.

rows: A ticket is created from any channel.
Ticket fields change. In **Only when these fields change**, you can name the fields to watch.
The ticket's status changes. Use the **changed to** and **changed from** checks on the status.
The assignee or the team changes.
An agent sends a public reply.
The customer replies through any channel.
An internal or handover note is added.
An SLA target reaches its warning point.
Something happens on a customer account. The rule runs on the related or open tickets.
A set time passes. The rule checks open tickets every 5 minutes to 7 days.
Another system calls the rule's own web address with a ticket number.

sections.title: Rule conditions
intro: Conditions decide which tickets the rule acts on. A rule without conditions acts on every ticket for its trigger.
Each condition has a field, a check and a value. Select **Condition** to add one, or **Group** to add a group of conditions.

blocks.caption: Conditions for high-priority tickets from VIP contacts or Platinum customers.
blocks.alt: If card with two conditions joined by All (AND) and a nested group joined by Any (OR)

list: **All (AND)** means every condition in the group must be true.
**Any (OR)** means one true condition in the group is enough.
Groups can sit inside groups, up to four levels deep.
Select the bin icon to remove a condition. Select **Remove group** to remove a group.

rows: Exact values, such as a priority, status, team or customer.
**contains**, **does not contain**, **contains any of**, **starts with**, **ends with**
Words in text fields and tags.
A text pattern. Ask a technical colleague to write it.
Fields that are blank or filled in.
Time since a date, such as the last activity. Use them in scheduled rules.
What the triggering event changed, such as the status.

sections.title: Rule actions
intro: Actions run in the order listed in the **Then** card. Changes appear in the ticket history as **Automation:** followed by the rule name.
Text fields accept placeholders, such as `{{ticket.number}}` or `{{contact.name}}`. Select a placeholder chip under the field to insert it.

blocks.caption: The **Notify agents** action with its fields and the placeholder chips.
blocks.alt: Notify agents action with Recipients, Specific agents, Roles, Title and Message fields, placeholder chips and Severity

rows: Assigns an agent or team, or runs automatic routing again.
Moves the ticket to another department.
Escalates the ticket and notifies supervisors. It can also raise the priority.
Changes the priority or severity. SLA targets follow the new priority.
Changes the status. It is not allowed on blueprint tickets.
Fills in or clears a custom field.
Adds a note that only agents see.
Sends a reply template to the customer.
Adds agents as watchers, collaborators or specialists.
Creates a task or a linked child ticket.
Sends an in-app notification to chosen people.
Sends a message to the contact, the assignee or an address.
Calls another system's web address. Failed calls are retried.
Updates the related record in Wings ERP.
Asks a person or a role to approve something.
Lets the AI suggest a classification or write a summary.

sections.title: Run a rule on a schedule
sections.intro: A scheduled rule checks open tickets at a set interval. Use it for reminders and time limits, such as closing tickets that wait too long.
steps: Open the rule designer.

steps.caption: The **Scheduled** trigger with the **Run every (minutes)** field.
steps.alt: When card with the Scheduled trigger selected and Run every (minutes) set to 60

steps: In **Run every (minutes)**, enter a number from 5 to 10080.
In the **If** card, add a time condition, such as **older than (minutes)** on the last activity.
Add the actions, then select **Save draft**.
sections.result: After you publish and activate the rule, the list shows how often it runs. The designer shows the next run time.

blocks.warning: A scheduled rule without conditions acts on every open ticket on every run. **Check** warns you about this.

sections.title: Let another system start a rule
sections.intro: With the **Inbound webhook** trigger, another system can start a rule for a ticket. For example, your ERP can add a note when a payment arrives.
steps: Open the rule designer and select **Inbound webhook** in the **When** card.
Add the conditions and actions, then select **Save draft**.
Copy the **Webhook URL** that now appears in the **When** card.

steps.text: Copy the secret in the yellow box and select **Copy**.
steps.warning: The secret is shown only once. If you lose it, select **New secret** and give the new one to the other system.

steps: Give the address and the secret to the person who sets up the other system.
sections.result: The other system can now start the rule. Each call names a ticket by its number.
blocks: Values that the other system sends can be used in conditions and texts. In the **If** card, enter a field name and select **Add payload field**. In texts, use the placeholder `{{webhook.<field>}}`.

sections.title: Simulate a rule
sections.intro: A simulation shows what a rule would do to real tickets. It changes nothing on the tickets.
steps: Open the rule and select the **Simulate** tab in the side panel.
Choose **One ticket** and enter a **Ticket number**. Or choose **Most recent** and enter the **Number of tickets**, up to 50.
To test your unsaved edits, turn on **Use the unsaved changes in the editor**.

steps.caption: The **Simulate** tab before a run.
steps.alt: Simulate tab with One ticket and Most recent options, Number of tickets and Run simulation

sections.result: The panel shows how many tickets matched. Each ticket shows **Matches** or **No match**, the check of every condition, and each action as **would run** or **skipped**.

blocks.note: Simulations appear on the **Executions** tab with the status **Simulated**.

sections.title: Check and publish a rule
sections.intro: Publish a rule to make it live. Only the published version runs.
steps: Open the rule and select **Check**.
If a red box lists problems under **Fix these before publishing:**, fix each one.
Read any yellow warnings, such as a scheduled rule without conditions.
Select **Publish**.
Turn on the **Active** switch in the toolbar.
sections.result: The app shows **Published v1** (or the next version number). The toolbar shows **Live: v1**.

blocks.tip: To switch a rule off quickly, turn off its switch on the **Rules** tab. The app shows **Rule deactivated**.

sections.title: Compare and roll back rule versions
sections.intro: Every save of a rule is a version. Use the **Versions** tab to see what changed and to go back.

steps.text: Open the rule and select the **Versions** tab.
steps.caption: The **Versions** tab with the published version 1.
steps.alt: Versions tab showing v1 with the Published and in editor badges, its date, author, change note, Open and Diff

steps: To see what changed, select **Diff** on a version. Added lines start with + and removed lines start with -.
To load an old version into the editor, select **Open**.
To make a draft live, select **Publish** on it.
To return to an older published version, select **Roll back** on it and confirm.
sections.result: A rollback publishes the old definition again as a new version. The old version stays in the history.

sections.title: Rule conflicts
sections.intro: SupportDesk compares active rules that share a trigger. It flags rules that may undo each other's work.

list: Two rules set the same field to different values.
Two rules assign the same tickets to different people or teams.
One rule adds a tag that another rule removes.
A rule stops processing before another rule can run.

blocks: The **Rules** tab shows the number of conflicts. In the designer, the **Conflicts** tab explains each one and links to the other rule.

blocks.tip: Most conflicts go away when you change the order of the rules or add a condition.

sections.title: Change the order of rules
sections.intro: Rules with the same trigger run from top to bottom.
steps: Select **Automation** > **Rules**.
Clear **Search rules**. You cannot reorder while a search is active.
Drag a rule by its grip, or select the up and down arrows next to it.
sections.result: The new order applies to the next event.

sections.title: Delete a rule
sections.intro: Delete a rule you no longer need. To keep it for later, switch it off instead.
steps: Open the rule.
At the bottom, select **Delete rule**.
In the confirmation, select **Delete**.
sections.result: The app shows **Rule deleted**. The rule and its versions are gone. Its execution history stays.

sections.title: See why a rule ran and retry failed actions
sections.intro: Open a run to see each condition and each action. You can run failed actions again.
steps: Select **Automation** > **Executions**.
Filter the list if needed, then select **Apply**.

steps.caption: The **Execution details** panel for a scheduled rule that closed a ticket.
steps.alt: Execution details panel with the status, rule, trigger, ticket, times, the conditions table and two succeeded actions

sections.title: How blueprints work
intro: A blueprint guides tickets through fixed states, such as investigation, fix, release and closed. Each step can need fields, a comment or an approval.
Blueprints need the blueprints feature of your plan.

list: A blueprint applies to new tickets of a department, a category, or both. If several blueprints fit, the most specific one wins.
A state sets the ticket's status and substatus. One state is the starting state, and some are final states.
A transition moves the ticket from one state to another. It can check roles, ask for fields and comments, or need an approval.
Agents run transitions from the ticket's **Blueprint** tab. They cannot change the status of a blueprint ticket directly.

blocks: Administrators with the automation permission can still change the status directly. They can also select **Remove ticket from blueprint** on the ticket.

blocks.caption: The **Blueprints** tab with one published blueprint.
blocks.alt: Blueprints tab with numbered highlights on the ticket box with Open ticket blueprint, New blueprint, the blueprint name with its switch, its badges and its footer

callouts: Enter a ticket number and select **Open ticket blueprint** to see that ticket's progress.
**New blueprint** opens the blueprint designer.

The department, the category and the published version.

sections.title: Design a blueprint
sections.intro: Create a blueprint to make tickets follow a fixed process.
prerequisites: You have the **Manage automation rules and blueprints** permission.
The statuses and substatuses you need already exist in ticket configuration.
steps: Select **Automation** > **Blueprints**, then select **New blueprint**.
Enter the **Blueprint name**. Choose the **Department**, the **Category**, or both.
Select **Add state** for each step of the process, then fill in each state in the **Inspector**.
Turn on **Initial state (new tickets start here)** for the first state, and **Final state** for the last ones.
Select a state, select **Connect from selected**, then select the target state.
Select each transition and fill in its fields in the **Inspector**.
Select **Check** and fix any problems it lists.
Select **Save draft**, then select **Publish**.
Turn on the **Active** switch.
sections.result: The app shows **Published v1**. New tickets that match the department or category follow the blueprint.

sections.title: Turn off, version or delete a blueprint
sections.intro: Blueprints have the same versions as rules.
steps: To stop a blueprint for new tickets, turn off its switch on the **Blueprints** tab.
To see older versions, open the blueprint and select the **Versions** tab.
On a version, select **Open** to load it, **Diff** to compare it, or **Publish** to make a draft live.
To delete a blueprint, open it without selecting anything on the canvas. Select **Delete blueprint** in the **Inspector** and confirm.
sections.result: The app confirms each change with a message.

blocks.note: **Delete blueprint** is greyed out while open tickets follow the blueprint. Close or move those tickets first.

sections.title: How webhooks work
intro: A webhook sends a message to another system each time something happens in SupportDesk. Examples are a new ticket, a customer change or a published article.
Every message is signed with a secret. The receiving system uses the signature to check that the message came from SupportDesk.
blocks: To open webhooks, select **Administration** > **Webhooks**, or the **Webhooks** tab on the **Automation** page. You need the permission to manage integrations.

blocks.caption: The **Webhooks** page with one disabled example webhook.
blocks.alt: Webhooks page with numbered highlights on New webhook, the webhook details, its last delivery, its switch, Deliveries and the more actions menu

callouts: **New webhook** adds a webhook.
The name, status, address and events of the webhook.
When the last message was delivered, and the answer code.
The switch enables or disables the webhook.
**Deliveries** opens the delivery log.
The menu with **Edit**, **Send test ping**, **Rotate secret** and **Delete**.

rows: Recent deliveries failed. A red badge shows how many failed in a row.
Nothing is sent. You or SupportDesk switched the webhook off.

list: A failed delivery is retried, first after 30 seconds and finally after 12 hours.
After 8 attempts, the delivery stops with the status **Dead letter**.
After 20 failures in a row, SupportDesk disables the webhook and notifies administrators.
Webhooks cannot call addresses inside your own network unless your server administrator allows it.

sections.title: Add a webhook
sections.intro: Add a webhook to send SupportDesk events to your ERP, chat tool or data warehouse.
prerequisites: You have the web address of the receiving system.
steps: Select **Administration** > **Webhooks**, then select **New webhook**.
Enter a **Name**.
Enter the **Payload URL**, the full web address of the receiving system.
Under **Events**, tick the events to send. Or tick **All events (current and future)**.

steps.text: Optionally enter a **Signing secret** of at least 16 characters.
steps.note: If you leave it empty, SupportDesk creates one for you.

steps.caption: The **New webhook** panel with a name and an address filled in.
steps.alt: New webhook panel with Name, Payload URL, the Events list, Signing secret, Enabled and Create webhook

steps.text: Copy the signing secret from the yellow box and select **Copy**.
steps.warning: The secret is shown only once. Give it to the receiving system before you select **Dismiss**.

sections.result: The app shows **Webhook created**. Select **Send test ping** in the webhook's menu to test it.

sections.title: Edit, test or delete a webhook
sections.intro: Use the webhook's menu for changes and tests.

steps.text: Select the menu button at the end of the webhook's row.
steps.caption: The webhook menu.
steps.alt: Menu with Edit, Send test ping, Rotate secret and Delete

steps: Choose **Edit** to change the name, address, events or secret. Then select **Save**.
Choose **Send test ping** to send a test message now. The app shows **Ping delivered** or **Ping failed**.
Choose **Rotate secret** to create a new secret, then confirm. Copy the new secret from the yellow box.
Choose **Delete** and confirm to remove the webhook and its delivery log.
sections.result: The list shows the changed webhook.

blocks.warning: After **Rotate secret**, the receiving system rejects messages until it has the new secret.

sections.title: Check deliveries and redeliver
sections.intro: The delivery log shows every message sent by a webhook, with the answer from the receiving system.
steps: On the webhook's row, select **Deliveries**.
To filter the log, choose a status, such as **Failed (retrying)** or **Dead letter**.

steps.text: Select a delivery to open it.
steps.caption: The delivery log of a webhook that has not sent anything yet.
steps.alt: Deliveries panel with the status list, Refresh, Send test ping and the list of deliveries

steps: Read the attempts, the times, the **Response** and the **Payload**.
To send it again, select **Redeliver**.
sections.result: The app shows **Queued for redelivery**. Select **Refresh** to see the new attempt.

blocks.note: **Redeliver** is greyed out while the webhook is disabled. Fix the receiving system, turn the webhook on, then redeliver.

troubleshooting.problem: **Publish** stays greyed out, or a red box lists problems.
troubleshooting.cause: The rule or blueprint has errors, such as a missing action or an unknown field.
troubleshooting.fix: Select **Check**, then fix each item under **Fix these before publishing:**.

troubleshooting.problem: You cannot turn on a rule's switch.
troubleshooting.cause: The rule has no published version.
troubleshooting.fix: Open the rule and select **Publish** first.

troubleshooting.problem: A rule did not act on a ticket.
troubleshooting.cause: The conditions did not match, the rule was inactive, or an earlier rule stopped processing.
troubleshooting.fix: Open **Executions**, enter the ticket number and select **Details** on the run.

troubleshooting.cause: Rules started each other in a long chain, so SupportDesk stopped it.
troubleshooting.fix: Add a condition so that the rules do not trigger each other.

troubleshooting.cause: It is not a full web address, contains a user name or password, or points inside your network.
troubleshooting.fix: Enter a full public address that starts with https://.

troubleshooting.problem: The app says the signing secret is too short.
troubleshooting.fix: Enter a longer secret, or leave the field empty to let SupportDesk create one.

troubleshooting.cause: It failed 20 times in a row.
troubleshooting.fix: Fix the receiving system. Turn the webhook on, then redeliver the failed messages.

troubleshooting.cause: Open tickets still follow the blueprint.
troubleshooting.fix: Turn off the blueprint's switch. Delete it after its tickets are closed.

faq.q: Does a simulation change my tickets?
faq.a: No. It only shows what would happen. The run is recorded as **Simulated** on the **Executions** tab.

faq.q: Can a rule change the status of a blueprint ticket?
faq.a: No. The **Set status** action is not allowed on blueprint tickets. Use a blueprint transition instead.

faq.q: What happens to running tickets when I publish a new blueprint version?
faq.a: New tickets use the new version. Tickets already on the blueprint keep the version they started with.

glossary.definition: An automation that runs actions on a ticket when a trigger fires and the conditions match.
The event that starts a rule, such as a new ticket or a customer reply.
A check on a ticket field that must be true for a rule or transition to apply.
One check of a rule against one event, recorded on the **Executions** tab.
A fixed process of states and transitions that guides a ticket from start to finish.
A step that moves a blueprint ticket from one state to another.
A signed message that SupportDesk sends to another system when an event happens.
A shared secret that the receiving system uses to check that a webhook message came from SupportDesk.
A webhook delivery that failed every retry and is no longer sent automatically.
